items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S4865

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the family court act and the social services law, in
relation to removing special powers granted to the society for the
prevention of cruelty to children; and repealing certain provisions of
the criminal procedure law, the public officers law and the social
services law relating thereto


 PURPOSE :
Repeals special powers granted to the Society for the Prevention of
Cruelty to Children (SPCC), which are in direct conflict with the
authority of state and local child protective services.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :
1) Amends subdivision (i) of section 1012 of the family court act, by
removing SPCC's from the definition as a child protective agency;
2) Amends subdivision (a) of section 1024 of the family court act, by
removing SPCC's authority to take a child into protective custody;
3) Amends subdivision 1 of section 1034 of the family court act, by
removing SPCC's authority to conduct child abuse investigations;
4) Amends paragraph (a) of subdivision 1 of section 417 of the social
services law, by removing SPCC's authority to take a child into
protective custody;
5) Amends subdivision 2 of section 386 of the social services law, by
removing SPCC's authority to visit group homes at its discretion;
6) Amends subdivision 5 of section 372 of the social services law by
eliminating references to the SPCC;
7) Repeals subdivision 7-a of section 2.10 of the criminal procedure
law by removing SPCC members authorization as peace officers;
8) Removes the ability of SPCC in NYC to designate its members as
peace officers;
9) Removes the SPCC as being considered a duly authorized association
within which children may be placed;
10) Removes SPCC's authority to investigate reports of child abuse.

 JUSTIFICATION :
Societies for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (SPCC) were first
established in New York State in the mid-1870s, in response to a need
for protecting children from abuse and neglect. At that time, there
were no state laws or authorities to protect children from abusive
situations. For over a century these organizations helped to protect
the children of our state. However, with the enactment of the Child
Protective Services Act in 1973, the state assumed the role of
protecting children against abuse and neglect.

For nearly a decade there were competing interests in providing these
services between the State and the SPCCs.  When investigations in the
1980s uncovered many problems with the SPCCs, a law was passed which
prohibited the chartering of new SPCCs and a number of the existing
organizations either dissolved or changed the focus of their efforts.
Out of the existing 14 organizations that are or were SPCCs, only 3
claim that they provide any type of child protective services.

In July of 2001, the New York State Commission of Investigation
released a report that details many abuses of authority still
committed by agents of the SPCCs. On numerous occasions, it is
documented that the agents of the SPCCs have misrepresented themselves
as law enforcement officers by wearing uniforms, carrying shields, and
using parking placards, which falsely identified them as state law
enforcement. These agents have also been reported to have interfered
in police investigations, and to have asked school officials and
hospitals to contact them if they identify any cases of abuse rather
than informing the State hotline.

Despite these findings, SPCCs are still authorized to provide child
protective services, and without any State oversight or regulation.
The SPCCs played a very valuable role for the children of New York
State for more than a hundred years, and many of the services they
provide to the community are still very valuable and necessary.
However, there is no longer a place for the SPCCs to provide child
protective services, unless they have contracted with a local social
services district like any other agency. The laws put in place over a
hundred years ago are no longer necessary, and if anything, are
dangerous to the system which has been established by the State to
ensure the safety of all the children in New York State.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
2008: A.10516-A/S.3153

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.

law and the social services law relating thereto; and providing for

 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL : Repeals special powers granted to

protective services

 SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS :  1) Amends subdivision (i) of
section 1012 of the family court act, by removing SPCCs from the
definition as a child protective agency;

2) Amends subdivision (a) of section 1024 of the family court act, by
removing SPCCs authority to take a child into protective custody;

3) Amends subdivision I of section 1034 of the family court act, by
removing SPCCs authority to conduct child abuse investigations;

4) Amends paragraph (a) of subdivision I of section 417 of the social
services law, by removing SPCCs authority to take a child into
protective custody;

removing SPCC's authority to visit group homes at its discretion;

6) Amends subdivision 5 of section 372 of the social services law by

7) Repeals subdivision 7-a of section 2.10 of the criminal procedure
law by removing SPCC members authorization as peace officers;

8) Adds a new subdivision 7-a to section 2.10 of the criminal

9) Removes the ability of SPCC in NYC to designate its members as

10) Authorizes officers or agents of any SPCC in Rockland County to

11) Removes the SPCC as being considered a duly authorized association

12) Removes SPCC's authority to investigate reports of child abuse.

which time the legislature shall review the fiscal circumstances which
necessitated such exemption.

14) Sets an immediate effective date, provide that sections 8, 10 and
13 expire five years after the effective date.
